draft.shortGloss: to have; there is / there are; to have to
notes: Irregular in the present tense: eu tenho, você/ele/ela tem, nós temos, vocês/eles/elas têm (notice the circumflex accent in the plural 'têm', pronounced the same as 'tem').

Unlike English, which uses 'to be' for age, Portuguese uses 'ter': 'Eu tenho 20 anos' (I am 20 years old). For hunger, thirst, or cold, Brazilians usually say 'estar com' ('Estou com fome') rather than 'ter'.

senses.definition: To own, possess, or hold something, or to have a relationship with someone.

examples.text: Eu tenho um carro novo e dois irmãos.
examples.translation: I have a new car and two brothers.

senses.definition: Used in the singular form 'tem' (or past 'tinha') to say that something exists or is present in a place.

examples.text: Tem muita gente na festa hoje.
examples.translation: There are many people at the party today.
examples.emotion: observational and slightly excited about the crowd

senses.definition: Used with 'que' or 'de' before an infinitive verb to say that someone must do something.
To be of a certain age, or to experience a state or feeling.

draftBefore.shortGloss: to have; to own; to possess
notes: Ter is the most common way to say 'to have' in Portuguese, used for both ownership and general possession. It is an irregular verb, so memorize its present tense forms: tenho, tens, tem, temos, tendes, têm.

Unlike in some languages where you use 'to have' for age or physical sensations (like 'to be hungry'), Portuguese uses the verb 'ter' for these instead of 'ser' or 'estar'. For example, 'Eu tenho 20 anos' (I am 20 years old) or 'Eu tenho fome' (I am hungry).

senses.definition: To possess, own, or hold something in your hand or life.

examples.emotion: matter-of-fact and satisfied with the purchase

senses.definition: To experience a feeling, physical sensation, or a specific age.

examples.emotion: concerned and checking on someone who looks chilly

senses.definition: To indicate existence; to mean there is or there are.

examples.text: Tem muita gente na festa hoje.
examples.translation: There are many people at the party today.
examples.emotion: observational and slightly excited about the crowd
examples.note: In casual Brazilian Portuguese, 'tem' is very frequently used to mean 'there is' or 'there are', replacing the formal 'há'.

faults.why: Missing the essential A1/A2 sense 'ter que / ter de' (to have to, must).

faults.quote: Unlike in some languages where you use 'to have' for age
faults.why: Self-contradictory; says 'unlike languages that use to have, Portuguese uses ter (to have)'.
In Brazilian Portuguese, temporary sensations like cold/hunger normally take 'estar com' ('Está com frio?').
